Our approach

One magnetic-bead chemistry, every product

Every KodaPure kit and KreatBio service runs on the same silica-coated magnetic beads — bind, wash, elute. Fast, forgiving of dirty samples, and no cold chain.

  • Room-temperature reagents — no dry ice
  • No spin columns — no clogging on dirty samples
  • Scales from single tubes to 96-well plates

Our purpose

Most health, agriculture, and research decisions are made too late — after a patient worsens, an outbreak spreads, a crop is lost, or months of work fail, because the simplest question comes last: what is actually in the sample?

KreatBio exists to move that question earlier. We build the tools and run the services that let laboratories across Southeast Asia turn a sample into reliable molecular evidence quickly, without importing an instrument park or a cold chain. When good molecular work is routine rather than reserved for a crisis, teams make fewer blind decisions and waste less time, money, and material.

Our science

We work across the whole molecular-biology workflow, from a raw sample to a clean answer. That means the kits and reagents that pull DNA and RNA out of hard, real-world samples; the laboratory that runs extraction, quantification, sequencing, and analysis; and the bioinformatics that turns raw reads into something you can act on.

Our range covers many sample types — microbes, plants, soil, animal tissue, food, and the environment — and both short-read and long-read sequencing. Magnetic-bead purification is one part of it, chosen because it is fast, forgiving of dirty samples, and works at room temperature. The through-line is simple: the workflow you buy is the workflow we run in our own lab, so a result behaves the same on your bench as it does on ours.

Our approach to molecular science

A few positions shape the decisions we make — about what to build, how to run it, and what to promise.

Evidence before the crisis

Sample-to-data capability should exist before an emergency, not be assembled during one. Routine surveillance, validation, and quality checks catch problems while they are still small and inexpensive to fix.

Access is capability

Widening access to molecular tools is market-building, not charity. When a regional lab can generate its own data instead of shipping every sample abroad, more research gets finished and more local expertise is created.

Precision starts with the question

The right workflow follows a clearly defined biological question, not the other way round. More data does not create more clarity if the sampling, controls, or method were wrong to begin with.

Computation serves the biology

Automation is for the repetitive work: quality checks, standard reports, routine classification. High-impact and unusual results still need a scientist who understands the limits of the data.

Claims should match the validation

Evidence standards should fit the intended use, and research-use work should never be dressed up as a clinical claim. We say what a method detects, what it does not, and how a result should be read.

Responsible science is disciplined science

Less avoidable waste and careful handling of your data are not a side project. Waste is a cost and a quality issue as much as an environmental one.

Who we serve

Molecular questions show up across the whole living world, so our work spans human and animal health, agriculture and aquaculture, food safety, environmental monitoring, academic research, and industry.

Our focus is Southeast Asia, where dense cities, heavy food production, rich biodiversity, cross-border trade, and climate exposure create complex monitoring needs. Building that capacity close to the samples means faster answers and more learning kept in the region.

Microbiome & microbial

Microbial DNA work lives or dies on two things: pulling DNA out of every organism in a sample rather than only the easy ones, and keeping inhibitors out so PCR and sequencing behave. Faeces, biofilms, and low-biomass swabs are where most protocols fall over.

KodaPure magnetic-bead chemistry captures nucleic acid across Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, fungi, and archaea, with a dedicated wash scheme for inhibitor-rich material. The same DNA feeds 16S or ITS amplicon and shotgun sequencing, and our team can carry it through to a finished community profile.

A profile you can trust

The recovered community should match what went in — not what was easiest to extract.

Things to weigh

16S/ITS or shotgun metagenomics?

16S and ITS are more affordable and scale to many samples for “who is there.” Shotgun costs more but adds function, resistance genes, and non-bacterial members like fungi and viruses.

Fresh or frozen?

Freeze soon after collection and avoid repeated freeze–thaw. Long storage at room temperature can shift the community before you extract, changing the answer.

How many samples vs how much depth?

Community studies live on replication and controls. More biological replicates usually tell you more than deeper sequencing of a few samples.

Sample types and handling

Pure cultures
Microbe kit (KBTNA-M-26); standard lysis for bacteria and fungi.
Stool / gut
Dirty-samples kit (KBTNA-MD-26); extended washes for bile salts and polysaccharides.
Environmental swabs
Low biomass — minimise contamination and always include controls.
Biofilms
Mechanical disruption (bead-beating) improves lysis of the matrix.
Fungi & yeast
Bead-beating recommended to break tough cell walls.
RNA work
Stabilise at collection with KodaProtect and keep samples cold — RNA breaks down much faster than DNA.

Plant & soil

Plant tissue and soil are among the hardest matrices in molecular biology. Leaves carry polysaccharides and polyphenols that co-precipitate with DNA; soil carries humic acids that shut down polymerase. Raw yield is easy — amplifiable yield is the real test.

KodaPure Plant and Soil kits pair mechanical disruption with a wash scheme tuned to strip these inhibitors, giving DNA ready for barcoding, genotyping, and sequencing. For soil communities, the same DNA supports 16S or shotgun metagenomics.

DNA that still amplifies

Leaf, seed, and soil are full of PCR inhibitors; the DNA has to work anyway.

Typical amplicon PCR success on inhibitor-rich material (polyphenols, humic acids), n = 12. Clean-up keeps amplification high where uncleaned extracts fail.

Things to weigh

Bead-beating or liquid nitrogen?

Bead-beating is fast and needs little equipment. Liquid-nitrogen grinding usually gives higher yield and integrity for waxy, fibrous, or tough leaves.

Which inhibitor is the problem?

Plants bring polysaccharides and polyphenols; soil brings humic acids. Match the kit to the matrix and add a wash step when the A260/230 ratio is low.

Barcoding or whole-genome?

ITS or 16S barcoding answers “what is present.” Whole-genome or targeted sequencing is for variants, resistance, or finer genetic detail.

Sample types and handling

Leaf / young tissue
Plant kit (KBTNA-P-26); young leaves generally give cleaner DNA.
Seed / fibrous tissue
Bead-beating, or liquid-nitrogen grinding for higher yield and integrity.
High-polyphenol species
An extra wash step improves the A260/230 ratio.
Soil / compost
Soil kit (KBTNA-S-26); extended washes remove humic acids.
Fertiliser
Treat as high-inhibitor; reduce input mass to avoid viscous lysate.
RNA work
Stabilise at collection with KodaProtect and keep samples cold — RNA breaks down much faster than DNA.

Things to weigh

Fresh, frozen, or preserved?

Intact, high-molecular-weight DNA needs gentle handling and cold storage. Rough handling shows up later as short fragments and poor sequencing libraries.

How much input?

Match input mass to your library requirement. For small or precious samples, reduce input and elute in a low volume to concentrate the DNA.

Targeted panel or whole-genome?

Targeted panels answer specific questions inexpensively. Whole-genome sequencing is for discovery, assembly, and broad variant calling.

Sample types and handling

Soft tissue / organs
Animal kit (KBTNA-A-26); keep samples cold until lysis.
Muscle / fibrous tissue
Thorough homogenisation is needed for full release.
Cultured cells
Pellet and lyse; gentle handling preserves DNA length.
Small / precious samples
Reduce input and elute in a low volume to concentrate.
RNA work
Stabilise at collection with KodaProtect and keep samples cold — RNA breaks down much faster than DNA.

Things to weigh

Where is the biomass?

Water and surveillance swabs are often low-biomass. Concentrate the sample on a filter before extraction and include negative controls throughout.

Barcoding or shotgun?

Barcoding identifies a target species inexpensively. Shotgun sequencing detects unknown pathogens and resistance genes but needs more sequencing depth.

One sample or a programme?

Surveillance is most useful when you decide in advance where to sample, how often, and who acts on the result — not one sample at a time.

Sample types and handling

Food matrices
Match the kit to the sample and homogenise well before lysis.
Water / filters
Concentrate biomass on a filter before extraction.
Surveillance swabs
Low biomass — include negative controls throughout.
AMR screening
Shotgun sequencing detects resistance genes directly.

Things to weigh

mRNA-seq or total RNA-seq?

mRNA-seq (poly-A) is the standard, more affordable choice for animals and plants. Total RNA-seq (rRNA depletion) is for bacteria, degraded RNA, and non-coding RNA. Tell us your organism and question and we will recommend one.

How many replicates do I need?

More biological replicates beat deeper sequencing of a few samples. Three per group is a common minimum; we will advise for your design.

Fresh, frozen, or stabilised?

Stabilise at collection with KodaProtect and keep RNA frozen until shipping. RNA breaks down fast, so speed and cold matter more than they do for DNA.

Diagnostics

Molecular information should arrive before the crisis

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph for a diagnostics article. A scientist (Southeast Asian, lab coat) studying a soft, out-of-focus colour glow with no readable content on a monitor in a modern clinical lab, face lit by the screen, thoughtful expression. Over-the-shoulder framing, screen and profile sharp, lab softly blurred behind. Mixed cool screen glow and soft ambient light. Shallow depth of field. Calm, analytical, high-stakes-but-controlled mood. Teal and navy palette. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Healthcare and life-science decisions are often made too late. A patient has already deteriorated, an outbreak has already widened, a crop disease has already spread, or a research program has already consumed months before the most important question is asked: what is actually present in the sample?

Molecular analysis changes that timing. It allows teams to move from assumption to evidence. Instead of waiting for visible symptoms, culture results, field losses, or repeated experimental failure, scientists and clinicians can read biological signals earlier and act with more confidence.

The central lesson from recent global health emergencies is not simply that the world needs more emergency testing. The better lesson is that sample-to-data capability should be available before emergencies begin. Laboratories, hospitals, universities, food producers, environmental agencies and biotechnology companies all benefit when they can generate reliable molecular evidence quickly.

For KreatBio, this means treating diagnostics and sequencing as everyday infrastructure. A good laboratory network should not sit idle until a crisis. It should support routine surveillance, research validation, product development, quality control and faster decision-making across health, agriculture, aquaculture, biodiversity and environmental work.

Better information also reduces waste. It can prevent unnecessary treatment, avoid repeating failed experiments, help identify contamination, narrow the search for pathogens and guide researchers toward the right next step. The value is not only scientific. It is operational: fewer delays, fewer blind decisions and better use of limited budgets.

The future of testing should therefore be judged by usability as much as by technical performance. Speed and accuracy matter, but so do access, sample logistics, interpretation, cost, and clear reporting. A result that arrives too late or cannot be understood by the decision-maker has only partial value.

Molecular tools will continue to improve, but the bigger shift is cultural. Organizations need to ask biological questions earlier, build testing into planning, and use data before problems become expensive. That is how molecular information becomes a practical asset rather than a last-minute response.

Sustainability

Sustainable science starts with small design choices

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph illustrating sustainable lab practice. A tidy minimalist lab bench with only a few reagent bottles, a reusable tube rack, and a white magnetic rack, deliberately little single-use plastic, a small potted plant at the edge. Wide clean composition, lots of empty bench and negative space. Soft morning daylight, warm and airy. Shallow depth of field. Thoughtful, calm, responsible mood. Muted greens with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents on white. No text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Modern laboratories create knowledge, but they also consume materials, energy and logistics capacity. Every extraction, sequencing run, freezer cycle, shipment, reagent box and disposable tube leaves a footprint. The question is not whether science should continue. It must. The question is how laboratories can reduce avoidable waste without compromising reliability.

Sustainability in life sciences is often discussed at a corporate level: targets, reporting, disclosures and procurement policies. Those are necessary. But practical progress usually begins much closer to the bench. A researcher chooses the right sample volume. A lab manager consolidates orders. A team validates a workflow that reduces repeat runs. A company designs packaging that uses less material. A facility reviews cold-chain energy use. Each change looks small until it is repeated thousands of times.

KreatBio’s view is that sustainable science should be integrated into workflow design, not added afterward as a communication exercise. If a process produces unnecessary plastic waste, excess transport, repeated failures or avoidable energy use, the process itself needs improvement.

This is not only an environmental issue. Waste is also a cost issue and a quality issue. Failed experiments consume reagents. Poor sample handling forces reruns. Unclear instructions increase errors. Better design can reduce waste and improve scientific output at the same time.

The industry should also be realistic. Laboratories depend on sterility, traceability and contamination control. Many materials cannot simply be replaced without validation. Sustainability efforts should therefore be evidence-based: measure the impact, test the alternative, protect quality and then scale the change.

A more sustainable laboratory sector will not be built through slogans. It will come from better planning, smarter procurement, validated low-waste workflows, training, and collaboration among researchers, suppliers, institutions and service providers. Responsible science is not separate from good science. It is one way good science proves its discipline.

Bioinformatics

Computation must serve the biology

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph for a bioinformatics article. A researcher at a clean workstation, a soft, out-of-focus colour glow with no readable content on a large monitor, an open paper lab notebook and coffee beside the keyboard. Over-the-shoulder three-quarter view, screen and hands sharp, room softly blurred. Warm desk-lamp light mixed with cool monitor glow. Shallow depth of field. Focused, intelligent, quietly busy mood. Teal and navy palette with warm accents. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Modern sequencing produces more information than most teams can review manually. The challenge is no longer only to generate reads. It is to convert raw output into a defensible answer that matches the scientific question.

This is where computational support becomes valuable. Automated checks can flag weak samples, summarise run quality, compare organisms, organise annotations and prepare draft tables for expert review. These tools are useful because they reduce repetitive work and help teams focus on interpretation.

They are not a substitute for experimental judgment. A poor sampling plan, contaminated input, insufficient controls or the wrong analysis method cannot be rescued simply by adding software. The best digital workflow begins with good biology and ends with a scientist who understands the limits of the result.

KreatBio’s view is that automation should be introduced where it improves consistency. Repeated quality-control steps, standard reporting formats, literature triage and routine classification tasks are good candidates. High-impact conclusions, unusual findings and customer-specific interpretations still require human review.

Governance is also essential. Project data must be stored securely, analysis parameters should be traceable, and customers should know which parts of the workflow are automated and which parts are reviewed by specialists. Without that transparency, speed can weaken confidence.

The strongest laboratories will be those that combine wet-lab discipline with informatics capability. Instruments create files; people create meaning. Digital tools should help the team move faster from sample to decision, while preserving scientific accountability at every step.

Data & security

Biological data needs security by design

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic conceptual editorial photograph about biological-data security. A closed laptop with a small padlock resting on it beside a second screen showing an abstract DNA-helix data visualisation, on a dim lab-office desk. Low three-quarter angle, shallow focus on the padlock, screen glow bokeh behind. Moody low-key lighting, cool blue and teal tones, one warm highlight. Secure, serious, modern mood. Deep-navy and teal palette, plenty of shadow. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Laboratories now generate more than physical results. They create datasets, sample records, sequence files, customer information, research findings and intellectual property. As more workflows move into cloud platforms, connected instruments and shared analysis environments, biological data becomes a security asset.

This creates a simple responsibility: protect the data before there is a problem. Cybersecurity in life sciences should not be treated as an IT add-on or a final compliance step. It should be built into how samples are received, how files are transferred, how results are stored, how access is granted and how reports are delivered.

The risk is broader than targeted attacks. A laboratory can be affected by weak passwords, misdirected files, outdated software, unsecured devices, third-party platform failures, phishing, accidental sharing or poor permission controls. In many cases, the practical risk begins with ordinary workflow gaps rather than sophisticated attackers.

Good protection starts with reducing exposure. Teams should know what systems are connected, who can access them, what data is stored, where backups sit and which third parties touch the workflow. Access should be limited to the people who need it. Sensitive files should move through controlled channels. Staff should be trained to recognise common threats.

For a molecular services company, trust depends on more than generating accurate data. Customers need confidence that their samples, projects and results are handled responsibly. This is especially important when work involves unpublished research, commercial development, biodiversity data, institutional collaborations or potentially sensitive biological information.

Security will never be finished. New tools, customers, partners and analysis methods create new exposure points. The right mindset is continuous review: map the risk, close the obvious gaps, test procedures, train people and make secure behavior easy to follow. In modern science, data protection is part of scientific quality.

Surveillance

Neglected biological threats do not stay neglected forever

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph about biological surveillance. Rows of blank, unlabelled environmental sample tubes in a rack on a bench, with a softly-blurred wall monitor showing only a soft glow with no readable content. Eye-level angle, tubes sharp in front, dashboard as glowing background context. Cool even lab light with screen glow. Shallow depth of field. Watchful, systematic, early-warning mood. Muted palette, teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents, a subtle soft amber glow. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Some biological threats attract attention only after they have become difficult to control. Slow-moving infections, environmental pathogens, antimicrobial resistance, animal disease, crop disease and contaminated supply chains can remain under-monitored for years because they do not always create immediate headlines.

That is a dangerous habit. Biology does not wait for funding cycles, institutional boundaries or public attention. A pathogen can move through people, animals, water, food systems or trade networks long before decision-makers recognise the pattern.

The problem is rarely a complete lack of scientific tools. In many cases, the tools exist: molecular detection, sequencing, resistance profiling, metagenomics, environmental sampling and data analysis. The larger weakness is deployment. Testing may be too limited, sample logistics may be poor, surveillance may be fragmented, and budgets may arrive only after damage is visible.

A better approach is to monitor earlier and more consistently. This does not mean testing everything all the time. It means identifying high-risk settings, choosing practical sampling strategies, using appropriate molecular methods and connecting the results to action. Surveillance has value only when someone is prepared to respond.

KreatBio sees this as a shared responsibility across public health, universities, industry, agriculture, aquaculture and environmental management. The same molecular capabilities that support research can also support preparedness. They can help detect unusual signals, understand transmission, identify resistance markers and guide containment.

The lesson is direct: underinvestment in detection creates larger costs later. Early molecular evidence is more affordable than late crisis management. Organizations that build surveillance capacity before they need it will be better positioned when the next biological risk becomes visible.

People & careers

Careers in science should move sideways as well as upward

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic candid editorial photograph for a careers article. Two scientists of different specialties collaborating at a lab bench, one in a lab coat gesturing at a sample, the other holding a laptop showing plots, both engaged and smiling slightly. Natural three-quarter framing, both faces visible, lab softly blurred behind. Warm soft daylight, gentle rim light. Shallow depth of field. Collaborative, human, growth-minded mood. Teal and navy palette with warm skin tones. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Scientific organizations often talk about talent as if careers move in one straight line. In reality, strong teams are built by people who cross boundaries: a wet-lab scientist who learns bioinformatics, a quality specialist who moves into operations, a field application colleague who becomes a product lead, or a researcher who develops customer-facing skills.

These moves are not detours. They create people who understand more than one part of the value chain. In a molecular services business, that matters. A sample does not pass through one function only. It moves through collection, extraction, sequencing, data processing, interpretation, reporting and customer communication. Teams work better when people understand the handoffs.

Organizations should therefore make internal mobility easier. Managers should ask what employees want to learn, not only what role they currently fill. Employees should be encouraged to signal interest early, take on cross-functional projects and build skills before a formal opening appears.

For individuals, the main requirement is preparation. A career change inside science still requires proof of capability. That may mean taking a short course, joining a project outside one’s usual scope, learning a new platform, documenting process improvements or shadowing another team.

For employers, the benefit is retention and resilience. Internal candidates already understand the culture, customers and operating constraints. They may need technical training, but they often bring institutional memory that external hires do not have.

A good science career is less like a ladder and more like a network. Progress can mean broader judgment, deeper expertise, wider exposure or greater ownership. The best organizations help people move where their skills can create the next layer of value.

Quality

Trust in testing depends on clear evidence standards

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph about quality and evidence. A quality specialist (gloved) examining a printed certificate of analysis on a clipboard beside a benchtop instrument and a KodaPure-style kit box in a clean, orderly lab. Close three-quarter angle, document and hands sharp, instruments softly blurred. Crisp even daylight, clean shadows. Shallow depth of field. Precise, rigorous, trustworthy mood. Muted white-and-steel palette with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

A test result can influence major decisions: whether to start treatment, repeat an experiment, release a batch, investigate contamination, change a breeding program or continue a research direction. Because the result carries weight, the evidence behind it must be clear.

This is why standards matter. A method should not be judged only by whether it produces a signal. Users need to know what the method detects, what it does not detect, what controls were used, what the limit of detection is, how reproducible the workflow is and how results should be interpreted.

In fast-moving fields, new assays and analysis methods can appear quickly. Innovation is valuable, but speed without transparency can weaken trust. Customers and stakeholders should be able to distinguish between exploratory research, internally validated workflows, clinically validated methods and regulated diagnostic claims.

KreatBio’s position is practical: evidence standards should fit the intended use. A research-use workflow may not require the same documentation as a clinical diagnostic test, but it still needs clear methodology and quality controls. A commercial test used for high-impact decisions should meet a higher bar. Claims should match the validation.

Good governance also supports innovation. When users understand performance, limitations and proper use, they are more likely to adopt new methods responsibly. Clear standards reduce confusion, protect end users and help serious providers differentiate themselves from weak claims.

The future of molecular testing will include more complex panels, faster sequencing, lower-cost analysis and wider deployment outside traditional laboratories. As access expands, trust must expand with it. That requires transparency, documentation, appropriate validation and communication that does not overstate what the data can prove.

Surveillance

Genomic surveillance should look beyond the obvious sample

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph about looking beyond the obvious sample. A gloved field scientist collecting an unusual environmental sample such as wastewater or pond water into a blank, unlabelled sterile bottle outdoors near infrastructure, focused expression. Low three-quarter angle, bottle and hands sharp, environment softly blurred. Natural overcast daylight, muted tones. Shallow depth of field. Investigative, resourceful, quietly urgent mood. Muted greens and greys with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Outbreak detection is often framed around patients, but biological signals appear in many places before they become obvious. Wastewater, livestock, aquaculture systems, soil, food-processing environments, wildlife, hospital surfaces and research facilities can all contain early clues.

Genomic surveillance helps turn those clues into intelligence. By sequencing and comparing biological material over time, teams can see whether a known organism is changing, whether an unexpected species is present, whether resistance markers are emerging, or whether contamination has entered a process.

The most useful surveillance systems are designed before the emergency. They define where to sample, how often to sample, which methods to use, what quality thresholds matter, who reviews the data and what action should follow. Without those decisions, sequencing can become a data-generation exercise rather than a decision tool.

Surveillance also needs local capacity. Sending every sample far away creates delays and weakens learning. Regional laboratories, universities and service providers can play an important role by building routine competence in extraction, sequencing, analysis and reporting.

This is especially relevant in Southeast Asia, where biodiversity, urban density, food production, trade, climate exposure and cross-border movement create complex biological monitoring needs. A stronger regional genomics ecosystem would support public health, environmental management, agriculture, aquaculture and academic research at the same time.

The goal is not to predict every threat. That is impossible. The goal is to shorten the time between biological change and human response. Genomic surveillance is valuable because it gives decision-makers an earlier signal — and earlier signals create more options.

Access

Access to molecular science is a business issue, not only a social issue

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic editorial photograph about access to molecular tools. A small regional research-lab team (Southeast Asian) using a KodaPure-style magnetic-bead kit at a modest but clean bench, one pipetting, one recording results, both engaged. Eye-level wide-ish shot, approachable and real, everyday lab rather than glossy showroom. Bright natural daylight, warm and honest. Shallow depth of field. Inclusive, practical, empowering mood. Muted palette with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents. No readable text or logos. 16:9 landscape. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Advanced molecular tools are often concentrated in well-funded institutions. Smaller laboratories, emerging biotech companies, regional universities and applied research teams may have strong scientific questions but limited access to instruments, trained personnel or bioinformatics support.

Closing that gap is not charity. It is market development. When more organizations can use molecular tools effectively, more research is completed, more products are validated, more ecosystems are monitored and more local expertise is created. The scientific market becomes broader and more capable.

Service models can help. Not every organization needs to own every instrument or hire every specialist immediately. A reliable partner can provide extraction, sequencing, quantification, analysis and reporting while customers build their own internal capability over time. This lowers the barrier to entry and helps projects move forward sooner.

Affordability matters, but price is not the only access issue. Turnaround time, sample requirements, report clarity, training, consultation and practical troubleshooting all shape whether customers can actually use the data. A low-cost result that is difficult to interpret may not create value.

KreatBio’s role is to support a healthier molecular ecosystem in the region: researchers who can test ideas faster, companies that can validate products more confidently, and institutions that can generate local data rather than relying entirely on distant infrastructure.

Sustainable access also requires a viable business model. Service providers must be able to invest in quality, people, maintenance and new methods. Customers must receive dependable outputs. The strongest model is a virtuous cycle: better access creates more demand, demand supports better capability, and better capability helps the scientific community do more ambitious work.

Precision

Precision starts with asking a better biological question

By KreatBio Leadership Team · Our Views
Photo to generatePhotorealistic macro editorial photograph about precision. Extreme close-up of a steady blue-nitrile-gloved hand positioning a single-channel pipette tip precisely at the rim of a 0.2 mL PCR tube, a droplet about to release, other tubes blurred in an array below. Tight macro framing, razor-thin focus on the tip and droplet, everything else soft bokeh. Soft directional light, crisp specular highlight on the droplet. Deliberate, meticulous, disciplined mood. Teal and navy accents on white. No text or logos. 16:9 macro. Constraints: no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, or watermarks anywhere; any screen is switched off, glared, or fully out of focus with no readable content; all tube and bottle labels are blank and featureless. Realistic, scientifically accurate lab equipment with correct proportions and no fantasy or impossible devices; correct anatomy with well-formed hands (exactly five fingers). Natural materials and texture, believable reflections and liquid menisci; avoid an over-smooth plastic look. KreatBio palette only: white and steel neutrals with teal (#007C78) and deep-navy accents.

Precision is often associated with advanced technology, but it begins earlier than that. Before choosing a sequencing platform or analysis pipeline, a team needs to define the biological question clearly. Are we identifying a species? Comparing microbial communities? Detecting variants? Confirming contamination? Studying genetic diversity? Monitoring resistance? Validating a product claim?

The answer determines the workflow. A poorly framed question can lead to the wrong sample type, insufficient replication, unsuitable sequencing depth, weak controls or an analysis that does not support the decision. More data does not automatically create more clarity.

This is why molecular projects need both technical execution and experimental thinking. DNA extraction quality affects downstream results. Library preparation choices shape what can be detected. Sequencing depth affects confidence. Bioinformatics parameters influence interpretation. Reporting determines whether the result can be acted on.

Precision also depends on context. A result may be technically correct but incomplete if the sampling plan is weak. A variant may be real but irrelevant to the user’s decision. A microbial profile may be interesting but not actionable. Good molecular science connects the result back to the original purpose.

For KreatBio, precision means helping customers choose the right path before work begins. Sometimes that means sequencing. Sometimes it means improving extraction. Sometimes it means quantification, pilot testing, controls, or a custom analysis plan. The best solution is not always the most complex one.

As molecular tools become more accessible, the differentiator will be judgment. Organizations that ask sharper questions, design better workflows and interpret data carefully will gain more value from the same technologies. Precision is not just a technical destination. It is a disciplined way of thinking from sample to decision.

Common questions

Practical answers to what teams ask most when running the kits.

My yield is low. What are the usual causes?

Usually too much or too little starting material, incomplete lysis (tough cells need bead-beating), or an old, degraded sample. Match your input to the table for that kit and make sure the sample is fully broken up.

My DNA will not amplify — PCR or qPCR keeps failing. Why?

Almost always residual inhibitors carried through from the sample. Add an extra wash, use less input for dirty samples, and check the A260/230 ratio — a low value means salts or organics are still present.

How much sample should I load?

Start in the middle of the input range listed for your kit. Overloading clogs the reaction and lowers purity, so more is not better.

Which kit do I use for stool or other dirty samples?

The Microbe – Dirty kit (KBTNA-MD-26). Its extra wash steps strip out bile salts and polysaccharides that block later reactions.

How do I store the kit and my eluted DNA?

The kit reagents sit at room temperature — no fridge or dry ice. Keep your eluted DNA cold (fridge for a few days, freezer for longer) and avoid freezing and thawing it over and over.

What purity should I expect?

For clean DNA, an A260/280 around 1.8–2.0 and an A260/230 around 1.8–2.2.

What equipment do I need?

A magnetic rack, something to break up the sample (a vortex or bead-beater), a small centrifuge, and a heat block. No spin columns and no vacuum manifold.

Can I scale up to a 96-well plate?

Yes. The bead chemistry works the same from a single tube up to a full plate.

Is the DNA ready for sequencing library prep?

Yes — it works for PCR, qPCR, and NGS library prep. Quantify it first so you load the right amount.

My plant or soil sample is thick, slimy, or brown. What now?

That is high polysaccharides, polyphenols, or humic acids. Use less input, add a wash step, and for tough tissue try grinding in liquid nitrogen.

Can I elute in a smaller volume to concentrate the DNA?

Yes. A smaller elution volume gives a higher concentration, which helps with small or precious samples.

Are these kits for clinical or diagnostic use?

No. They are for research use only, not for diagnosing or treating people or animals.

How it works

Lyse → bind RNA to magnetic beads → wash → on-bead or in-solution DNase → wash → elute in RNase-free buffer. A magnet holds the beads to the tube wall at each step, so there is nothing to clog and no spin column. Same handling as your DNA kits — if your team already runs KodaPure, they already know this.

Common questions

My RNA yield is low. What are the usual causes?

Usually the RNA had already started degrading before extraction, incomplete lysis (tough cells need bead-beating), or too much or too little input. Stabilise at collection with KodaProtect and match your input to the table.

Is the RNA free of genomic DNA?

The kit includes a DNase step that removes most genomic DNA carry-over. For very sensitive assays, run a no-RT control to check.

Why does my RNA look degraded on a gel or low on RIN?

RNA is fragile. The most common cause is a delay between collection and stabilising or extracting. Work fast, keep things cold after elution, and use KodaProtect in the field.

Do I need special water or tubes?

Use RNase-free consumables and the RNase-free buffer supplied. Once eluted, keep RNA on ice and freeze for storage.

Can I use it after preserving samples in KodaProtect?

Yes — that is the intended pairing. Lift the sample out, blot, and extract.

Do I need Proteinase K?

For the Tissue & Cell kit, yes, for full lysis — it is listed as required and not included. See KodaPK. The other kits do not need it.

What equipment do I need?

A magnetic rack, a way to break up the sample (vortex or bead-beater), a small centrifuge, and a heat block. No spin columns, no vacuum manifold.

Can I scale up to a 96-well plate?

Yes. The bead chemistry works the same from a single tube to a full plate.

Is the RNA ready for sequencing?

Yes — it is suitable for RT-qPCR and RNA-seq library prep. Quantify and check integrity (RIN) first, then send it to KodaSeq RNA if you would like us to run it.

Can I elute in a smaller volume to concentrate?

Yes. A smaller elution volume gives a higher concentration for small or precious samples.

Is this kit for clinical or diagnostic use?

No. It is for research use only.

Products

Reagents & consumables

The everyday reagents behind DNA and RNA work — sample preservation, freeze-dried PCR mixes, Proteinase K, and clean-up beads. Room-temperature where we can, so you skip the cold chain. For Research Use Only.

Request a quote →All products
KodaProtectKodaMixKodaPKKodaClean

KodaProtect

Lock in RNA the moment you collect it — a ready-to-use liquid you add fresh samples directly to, so the RNA stops breaking down without dry ice or liquid nitrogen. Room-temperature stable and non-toxic. Pairs with KodaPure RNA and KodaSeq RNA.

Catalogue no.ItemPrice
KBRP-100-26Preservation liquid, 100 mLMYR 210

*Indicative prices for planning; your quote confirms the final figure.

KodaMix

Ready-to-use master mixes that ship and store at room temperature. A master mix is the pre-blended reagent that runs your PCR — enzyme, building blocks, and buffer in one. Add water, primers, and template, and run — no −20 °C freezer.

Catalogue no.ItemPrice
KBMM-HS-500-262X Hot-Start Taq Master MixMYR 240
KBMM-QP-500-262X SYBR qPCR Master MixMYR 320
KBMM-RT-200-261-Step RT-qPCR Probe Master MixMYR 380

*Indicative prices for planning; your quote confirms the final figure.

KodaPK

The enzyme your extraction protocol calls for. Proteinase K breaks proteins down during lysis — opening cells and tissue and stopping the enzymes that would otherwise degrade your DNA and RNA. A highly pure, recombinant, nuclease-free grade, supplied as a ready-to-use solution or a room-temperature powder.

Catalogue no.ItemPrice
KBPK-SOL-10-26Solution, 20 mg/mL, 10 mLMYR 190
KBPK-SOL-25-26Solution, 20 mg/mL, 25 mLMYR 390
KBPK-PWD-1G-26Lyophilised powder, 1 gMYR 320

*Indicative prices for planning; your quote confirms the final figure.

Listed as required-but-not-included by the KodaPure RNA Tissue & Cell and Animal kits.

KodaClean

Clean up DNA before sequencing. After PCR or library prep, your DNA is mixed with primers, enzymes, salts, and stray short fragments. KodaClean is an SPRI-type magnetic-bead reagent that binds the DNA you want so you can wash the rest away, then releases it clean. Change the bead ratio to pick a size range. Magnet, no spin.

Common questions

What teams ask most about sending us samples.

What do I send you?

Your raw samples, or a lysate if you have one. We confirm the sample type, how much to send, and how to ship it before you post anything.

How should I ship my samples?

We agree the handling and any cold-shipping with you first, so nothing degrades on the way to us.

What do I receive?

Purified DNA in elution buffer, in labelled tubes, together with its quality-control results.

How long does it take?

Usually 2–3 working days once your samples reach the lab.

What sample types can you handle?

Microbes, soil, plant, animal tissue, and more — the same magnetic-bead chemistry as our kits.

Do you quantify the DNA as well?

We check yield and integrity. If you want full concentration and purity numbers, we can add our KodaQuant service.

Are my samples and results kept private?

Yes. Your material and data are confidential and never shared.

Can you extract and then sequence in one go?

Yes. We can hand the DNA straight to our KodaSeq sequencing service.

What happens if a sample fails or gives very little DNA?

We tell you exactly what we saw and suggest a next step — more input, a different prep, or a small pilot first.

Is this service for diagnostic use?

No. It is for research use only.

Common outputs, explained

These terms often appear in sequencing and microbiome reports. The goal is to show what changed, how diverse the sample is, and what the organisms may be able to do.

OutputWhat it meansWhy we do it
SNPA single nucleotide polymorphism is a one-letter DNA difference at a specific position in the genome.It helps compare isolates, track relatedness, detect strain differences, and identify mutations linked to traits such as resistance.
SNP IDThe exact position and base change for a SNP.It gives a precise marker that can be reported, compared across samples, or checked against known mutation databases.
Abundance bar chartA stacked chart showing the relative amount of each taxon in each sample.It quickly shows which bacteria, archaea, or fungi dominate and how community composition differs between samples.
Alpha diversity: Observed ASVs/OTUsThe number of unique sequence groups detected in one sample.It estimates richness: how many different microbes are present.
Alpha diversity: Chao1A richness estimate that gives extra weight to rare microbes.It helps estimate how many microbes may be present but were only lightly sampled.
Alpha diversity: ShannonA diversity score that considers both richness and evenness.It shows whether a sample has many microbes and whether they are balanced rather than dominated by one group.
Alpha diversity: SimpsonA diversity score focused on dominance.It helps show whether a few microbes dominate the sample.
Alpha diversity: Faith PDA diversity score that uses the evolutionary tree of the detected microbes.It shows how phylogenetically broad the community is, not just how many names are present.
Beta diversity: Bray-CurtisA distance measure based on abundance differences between samples.It shows whether two samples have different dominant community profiles.
Beta diversity: JaccardA distance measure based on presence or absence.It shows whether two samples contain the same kinds of microbes, regardless of abundance.
Beta diversity: Unweighted UniFracA phylogenetic distance using presence or absence.It shows whether samples contain different evolutionary groups of microbes.
Beta diversity: Weighted UniFracA phylogenetic distance that also includes abundance.It shows whether samples differ in both evolutionary groups and how much of each group is present.
Beta diversity: PCoA plotA 2D or 3D plot that places samples based on their beta diversity distances.It makes sample clustering easy to see, such as whether treatment groups, sites, or time points have different microbial communities.
Functional prediction via PICRUSt2A prediction of likely gene functions from 16S profiles.It provides an estimate of possible pathways, but it is not direct gene measurement like shotgun metagenomics.
Raw read QCSummary of read quality, read count, base quality, and trimming results.It confirms whether the sequencing data is clean enough for reliable analysis.
Sequencing depthHow many times, on average, each genome position is covered by reads.Higher depth improves confidence in assembly, SNPs, and mutation calls.
Genome coverageThe percentage of the genome represented by sequencing reads or assembled contigs.It shows whether the genome is mostly captured or has large missing regions.
Assembly statisticsGenome size, contig count, N50, GC content, and total assembled bases.It gives a quick quality check of how complete and fragmented the assembly is.
Contamination checkA screen for mixed organisms or unexpected DNA in the sample.It helps prevent wrong species ID, false gene calls, and misleading results.
MLST sequence typeA strain typing result based on standard housekeeping genes.It helps compare isolates using a common public typing system.
Serotype or lineageA predicted subtype or lineage, when supported by the organism and database.It helps classify strains for epidemiology, surveillance, or outbreak context.
AMR genes and mutationsDetected antimicrobial resistance genes and known resistance-associated mutations.It helps predict possible resistance traits and supports screening decisions.
Virulence genesGenes associated with pathogenicity, toxins, adhesion, invasion, or host interaction.It helps estimate potential risk factors carried by the isolate.
Plasmid repliconsMarkers showing likely plasmid types in the genome.It helps identify mobile DNA that can carry AMR or virulence genes.
Mobile genetic elementsProphages, insertion sequences, transposons, integrons, or related mobile regions.It shows how genes may move between bacteria or change genome structure.
CRISPR arraysRepeated immune-memory regions found in some bacterial genomes.They can support strain comparison and provide clues about past phage exposure.
Phylogenetic treeA tree showing how closely samples or isolates are related.It helps visualise clusters, likely related isolates, and evolutionary distance.
Genome completenessAn estimate of how much expected single-copy marker content is present.It helps judge whether a genome is complete enough for downstream interpretation.

Amplicon or whole-genome sequencing

Amplicon sequencing

Amplify and sequence one marker region — 16S for bacteria, ITS for fungi, or COXI for animals. The economical way to profile who is present across many samples.

Best for: community composition, large sample sets, tight budgets.

Whole-genome sequencing

Sequence the full genome of an isolate for assembly, variant calling, and annotation — down to strain-level detail.

Best for: bacterial isolates, resistance and virulence genes, strain typing.

Shotgun metagenomics

Sequence all the DNA in a sample for gene-level and functional information, covering bacteria, fungi, and viruses together.

Best for: function and pathways, AMR gene detection, non-bacterial members.

Common questions

What do I need to send?

Raw samples or DNA. We confirm sample concentration for your application before you ship.

What data do I receive?

FASTQ raw reads, FASTA reads, and the respective bioinformatics analysis report, with QC results and charts.

How long does it take?

On average, 4 to 8 weeks.

I would like to learn soil microbes. Should I do shotgun metagenomics or 16S metagenomics?

It depends on your budget and target. Shotgun metagenomics is more expensive and can produce many non-target or low-value DNA sequences, but it can support deeper questions such as metabolic pathways, antibiotic resistance, and broader gene-level profiling. 16S metagenomics is targeted, so it focuses on bacteria and archaea that the primers can amplify. If you mainly want to know which bacteria or archaea are present, 16S is usually the more practical choice.

I would like to understand my analysis report. Can I request for a data walkthrough?

Yes.

How much DNA do you need?

We confirm the amount and concentration for your specific application before you ship.

What if my DNA is low or degraded?

We will advise you. Sometimes re-extracting or changing approach gives much better libraries and a cleaner result.

16S, ITS, or COXI — which marker do I pick?

16S for bacteria, ITS for fungi, and COXI for animal barcoding.

What quality checks do you run?

Read quality checks throughout, and for whole genomes also coverage, assembly stats, and a contamination screen.

Can I get the raw reads?

Yes. You receive FASTQ raw reads and FASTA, plus the analysis report.

Is this service for diagnostic use?

No. It is for research use only.

How it works

A single strand of DNA (or RNA) is threaded through a tiny protein pore. As each base passes, it changes an electrical current in a way we can read and translate straight back into sequence — live, as it happens, with no limit on how long each read can be.

01

Sample received

You send raw sample or purified DNA/RNA. We confirm amount and quality before you ship.

02

Library prep & real-time sequencing

We prepare the library and load it onto the nanopore flow cell; reads stream in real time while analysis runs alongside.

03

Report delivered

You receive quality-controlled reads and a clear report. Optional data walkthrough.

What long reads add

Any read length

From short fragments to ultra-long reads — long enough to span repeats and close a genome in one piece.

Real-time data

Reads appear as they are generated, so results can begin within hours of loading rather than only at the end of a run.

Native molecule

DNA and RNA are read directly, so methylation comes with the sequence — no bisulfite step, no separate assay.

Species-level 16S

Reading the whole 16S gene, not one short region, resolves many organisms to species rather than stopping at genus.

Long-read approaches

Whole-genome & assembly

Sequence a full genome in long reads for a complete, closed assembly — plasmids, repeats, and structural changes included.

Best for: complete bacterial genomes, plasmids, structural variants.

Full-length 16S / ITS

Read the entire marker gene instead of one short region, for finer, species-level community profiling.

Best for: microbiome studies needing species resolution.

Shotgun metagenomics

Sequence all the DNA in a sample and recover near-complete genomes directly from mixed communities.

Best for: function, AMR genes, and non-bacterial members.

Direct RNA & isoforms

Sequence native RNA end to end for full-length isoforms and RNA modifications — no cDNA step.

Best for: transcript structure and isoform discovery. (Confirm this is offered.)

Accurate enough, and getting sharper

Current chemistry reads at over 99% per read, and consensus reads go higher — close to short-read for many uses.

Common questions

What can I send?

Raw sample or purified DNA/RNA. For long reads, gently handled, high-molecular-weight DNA gives the best results — we confirm requirements before you ship, and can extract for you if needed.

Why choose long reads over Illumina?

Long reads span repeats and whole genes, so they can close a genome, resolve plasmids and structural changes, and read the full 16S for species-level ID. For high-throughput counting of many samples, short-read KodaSeq is often the better fit.

Is the accuracy good enough now?

Yes for most applications. Current chemistry reads at over 99% per read, and consensus reads go higher — close to short-read for many uses.

Nanopore or PacBio HiFi?

Both give long reads. Nanopore adds portability, real-time data, direct RNA, and any read length; PacBio HiFi gives the highest per-read accuracy. We help you pick — ask a scientist.

Can I get methylation?

Yes — methylation (5mC, 5hmC, and more) is read directly with the sequence, with no extra assay. (Confirm this is offered.)

What data do I receive?

FASTQ raw reads, FASTA, and a bioinformatics report with QC, assembly or profiling, and charts.

Is this for diagnostic use?

No. For research use only.

How it works

The DNA is joined into a small circle and a polymerase reads around it again and again. Each molecule is read many times, then those passes are merged into one high-accuracy consensus — a “HiFi” read that is both long and precise.

01

Sample received

You send high-quality DNA (or raw sample). We confirm amount and quality — HiFi likes intact, high-molecular-weight DNA.

02

Library prep & HiFi sequencing

We build the circular library and run it; the instrument produces high-accuracy HiFi reads on board.

03

Report delivered

You receive HiFi reads and a clear report. Optional data walkthrough.

Why HiFi

Long and accurate

Reads tens of kilobases long at around 99.9% accuracy — long-read detail without the usual accuracy trade-off.

Complete assemblies

Long, accurate reads span repeats, so genomes assemble into near-complete, gap-free sequences.

Even, low-bias coverage

Little GC bias means more uniform coverage and fewer blind spots across the genome.

Exact 16S variants

Accuracy high enough to resolve exact sequence variants (ASVs) from the full-length 16S gene, to species level.

HiFi approaches

Whole-genome / de novo

Assemble a full genome from long, accurate reads — complete, phased, and annotated.

Best for: reference-grade genomes, structural variants, phasing.

Full-length 16S / rRNA

Read the whole marker gene at high accuracy for species-level, ASV-based community profiling.

Best for: high-resolution microbiome studies.

HiFi metagenomics

Recover high-quality genomes from complex communities using accurate long reads.

Best for: strain resolution, function, AMR.

Iso-Seq transcripts

Sequence full-length transcripts to map isoforms directly rather than inferring them.

Best for: isoform discovery and annotation. (Confirm this is offered.)

Long reads, short-read-grade accuracy

HiFi reads are built from many passes of the same molecule, so length and precision come together.

~99.9%
Median read accuracy (Q30) — low systematic error
15–25  kb
Typical HiFi read length
No  PCR
Native molecules — even, low-bias coverage
Typical: each extra pass of the same molecule raises accuracy. Around 4 passes reaches ~Q20; ~9+ reaches ~Q30 (99.9%).

Common questions

What is a HiFi read?

A long read built from many passes of the same DNA molecule, merged into one high-accuracy sequence — long and precise.

Why HiFi over Nanopore?

Both give long reads. HiFi’s strength is very high per-read accuracy, which suits reference-grade assembly and exact 16S variants. Nanopore adds portability, real-time data, and direct RNA. We help you choose.

Why HiFi over Illumina?

Long, accurate reads span repeats and whole genes — so they assemble complete genomes, resolve structural variants, and read the full 16S. For high-throughput counting, short-read KodaSeq can be more economical.

How much / what quality DNA do you need?

HiFi prefers intact, high-molecular-weight DNA and a higher input than short-read. We confirm the exact amount for your application before you ship — and can extract for you if needed.

Can I resolve species in a microbiome?

Yes. Full-length 16S at HiFi accuracy resolves many organisms to species, well beyond short-region genus-level.

What data do I receive?

HiFi reads (BAM), FASTA/FASTQ on request, and a bioinformatics report with QC, assembly or profiling, and charts.

Is this for diagnostic use?

No. For research use only.

Common outputs, explained

These terms appear in RNA-seq reports; the goal is to show what changed, and what it may mean.

OutputWhat it meansWhy we do it
Raw read QCRead count, base quality, and trimming summary.Confirms the data is clean enough to trust.
Alignment / mapping rateThe share of reads that match the reference.Low mapping can flag contamination or the wrong reference.
Gene counts (count matrix)A table of how many reads hit each gene per sample.The raw material for every expression comparison.
Normalisation (TPM/CPM)Counts adjusted so samples can be compared fairly.Removes differences in sequencing depth between samples.
Differentially expressed genes (DEGs)Genes that go up or down between your groups, with a fold-change and an adjusted p-value.Points you to the genes that actually change with your treatment, tissue, or condition.
Volcano plotA chart of fold-change vs significance.Shows the strongest, most reliable changes at a glance.
MA plotFold-change against average expression.Reveals whether changes cluster at high or low expression.
HeatmapA coloured grid of expression across samples and genes.Shows patterns and which samples group together.
PCA plotSamples placed by overall expression similarity.Checks that replicates cluster and groups separate.
Sample correlationHow similar each sample is to the others.Flags outliers or swapped samples early.
GO enrichmentGene-function categories over-represented in DEGs.Turns a gene list into biological meaning.
KEGG / pathway enrichmentBiological pathways over-represented in DEGs.Shows which processes your condition is affecting.
Novel transcripts (optional)Transcripts not in the reference annotation.Useful for non-model organisms and discovery work.
miRNA profile (small RNA)Known and novel microRNAs and their abundance.For regulatory-RNA and biomarker studies.

What your RNA-seq figures look like

The figures your report includes, shown with example data. Yours are made from your own results.

Which RNA-seq fits

mRNA sequencing (poly-A)

Captures messenger RNA via its poly-A tail. The economical, standard choice for gene-expression studies in eukaryotes.

Best for: routine gene expression, large sample sets, tight budgets.

Total RNA sequencing (rRNA depletion)

Removes ribosomal RNA and sequences the rest — coding plus many non-coding RNAs. Works where poly-A capture does not (bacteria, partly degraded RNA).

Best for: bacteria, non-coding RNA, degraded or FFPE-type samples.

Small RNA / microRNA sequencing

Sequences short RNAs such as microRNAs.

Best for: miRNA profiling, regulatory-RNA studies, biomarker discovery.

Common questions

What do I send you?

Purified RNA, or samples for us to extract. We confirm the amount and quality (RIN) needed for your application before you ship.

How much RNA do you need, and how good does it have to be?

It depends on the approach — we will confirm a minimum amount and RIN for your job. Higher-integrity RNA gives cleaner results, so stabilise at collection (KodaProtect) and keep RNA frozen until shipping.

mRNA-seq or total RNA-seq — which do I pick?

mRNA-seq (poly-A) is the standard, more affordable choice for gene expression in animals and plants. Total RNA-seq (rRNA depletion) is for bacteria, degraded RNA, or when you care about non-coding RNAs. Tell us your organism and question and we will recommend one.

How many replicates do I need?

For differential expression, more biological replicates beat deeper sequencing of a few samples. Three per group is a common minimum; we will advise for your design.

What data do I receive?

FASTQ raw reads, a gene-count matrix, normalised expression, differential expression tables, standard plots, pathway enrichment, and a written report.

How long does it take?

On average, 4–8 weeks once your samples reach the lab.

Can I just get the raw reads and do my own analysis?

Yes. You can take the FASTQ files and count matrix and stop there, or add custom analysis through KodaAly.

What if my RNA is low or degraded?

We will tell you what we see and suggest a next step — re-extraction, a different approach (e.g. total RNA-seq), or a small pilot first.

Do you handle the extraction too?

Yes. Send samples and we will extract with KodaPure RNA, then sequence — one handover, one report.

Is this service for diagnostic use?

No. It is for research use only.

What quality means at KreatBio

QC on every batch

Reagent lots are checked for binding performance and purity before they ship. Results are recorded and available on request.

Certificate of Analysis

A per-lot CoA documents the specifications your batch was tested against, so your methods section can reference an exact lot.

Traceable end to end

Catalogue numbers, lot codes, and protocol versions are tracked through each service run, giving you a clean audit trail for publication.

What our QC involves

Quality here is a test on the real chemistry, not a line on a form. Each reagent lot is made to a fixed recipe, run on a control sample, and released only if it meets spec.

Binding & yield
Each lot must pull down DNA from a control sample within a set range.
Elution purity
A260/280 and A260/230 ratios confirm the DNA is protein- and salt-clean.
Contamination
Lots are checked for obvious contamination before they are cleared.
On the record
Lot number, test results, and expiry are written to the lot record and the Certificate of Analysis.

Release testing, product by product

The same rule for every line: if we cannot test it and write it down, we do not claim it. Any component that needs cold storage says so.

KodaPure RNA
Binding and yield on a control, A260/280, DNase confirmation, and RNase-free release testing.
KodaMix
Amplification / Ct performance against a reference, with room-temperature stability on record.
KodaPK
Specific activity, plus nuclease-free (DNase and RNase) release testing.
KodaClean
Recovery and size-cut checked against a ladder, per lot.
KodaProtect
RNase-free release testing and stated shelf life; ships and stores at room temperature.

Research Use Only

“For Research Use Only” means these products are made and sold for research, method development, and quality control — not to diagnose, treat, or make clinical decisions about a person or animal.

That is an honest label, not a limit of the chemistry. It means we validate our kits for research performance and do not make clinical claims we cannot back. If you plan to use a workflow in a regulated or clinical setting, that validation is your responsibility — and we are glad to share what we know to support it.

Common questions

Do you need DNA or can you quantify from a raw sample?

We quantify purified DNA or RNA. If you need extraction first, our KodaXtract service can handle that and hand off straight to quantification.

How fast can I get results?

For urgent work, results can come back within a few hours. Standard turnaround is up to two working days.

How much sample do you need?

Only a few microlitres. We confirm the exact volume when you contact us.

What methods do you use?

Both fluorometric and spectrophotometric measurement on calibrated DeNovix instruments.

Which number should I trust for library prep?

The fluorometric one. It measures double-stranded DNA specifically and ignores most contaminants, so it reflects what actually enters your reaction.

What do the purity ratios mean?

A260/280 flags residual protein; A260/230 flags salts and organics. Both near 1.8–2.2 means the sample is clean.

Can you measure RNA too?

Yes — DNA or RNA.

My readings look off or keep changing. Why?

Usually contaminants, a degraded sample, or a concentration outside the method’s best range. We flag it when we see it.

Do you keep residual sample?

We return or discard it as you ask — nothing is kept without your say-so.

Is this service for diagnostic use?

No. It is for research use only.

Common questions

Do I need a PhD for R&D roles?

Not necessarily. Senior research roles usually expect an advanced degree, but we hire at many levels and weigh practical experience, clear thinking, and a genuine passion for the science just as heavily as formal credentials. Each posting lists the real minimum under "What you will bring".

What does your interview process look like?

Most roles follow four steps: a recruiter chat, a manager conversation, a skills or panel round (a technical exercise, presentation, or case, depending on the team), and a final values-and-team interview. We share the exact stages up front and keep you updated.

Are roles remote, hybrid, or on-site?

It depends on the work. Lab, manufacturing, and QC roles are on-site by nature. Most office-based roles are hybrid, usually 2-3 days on-site per week. Fully remote roles are labelled "Remote" in the listing and job description.

How long does the process take?

Two to four weeks from application to offer is typical, though it varies with scheduling and role. If timelines shift, we will tell you why and what comes next.

Do you sponsor visas or offer relocation?

For many roles, yes — it depends on the position and country, and it is noted in the working-conditions part of each job description. Please contact us whatever your current work status; we will be clear about what is possible.

What if I do not see a role that fits me?

KodaPure Chemistry R&D

R&D Scientist — Extraction Chemistry

Selangor, MalaysiaFull-timeSenior

About the role

Own and improve the magnetic-bead extraction chemistry behind every KodaPure kit and KreatBio service. You will take a formulation from a bench idea to a validated, room-temperature-stable kit that pulls clean, amplifiable DNA out of tough samples like soil, stool, and plant tissue.

What you will do

  • Design and optimise bead-based total nucleic-acid (DNA and RNA) extraction chemistry — bind, wash, elute — across different sample types.
  • Run structured experiments to define robust formulations that stay stable at room temperature.
  • Check performance carefully: yield, purity (A260/280 and A260/230), DNA integrity, and how well the DNA amplifies by qPCR.
  • Troubleshoot difficult, inhibitor-rich samples down to the real cause and fix them.
  • Write clear protocols, batch records, and validation reports.
  • Support hand-off of locked formulations to manufacturing and QC.
  • Work with the sequencing team so extracted DNA performs well downstream.
  • Guide junior scientists and review their experiments and notebooks.

What you will bring

  • Degree in a life-science or chemistry field with practical nucleic-acid extraction experience.
  • Strong molecular-biology skills: extraction, PCR/qPCR, and purity and integrity checks.
  • Experience developing or improving extraction methods (bead-based a plus).
  • Careful experimental design and clear data analysis.
  • Clear scientific writing.
